label: algebra & functions batch — exponentials, logs, factoring, systems, sequences, functions

widget.prompt: P(x) = 200·bˣ. Slide the base until b² reads 9 — the factor a tripling colony needs.
widget.successFeedback: Base 3, so b² = 9 and P(2) = 200·9 = 1800. The base IS the growth factor: tripling means multiplying by 3 once per year, and two years compounds it to 9.
widget.lowFeedback: b² is still under 9 — a colony growing this slowly is not tripling. Raise the base.
widget.highFeedback: b² has passed 9, so this colony more than triples each year. Lower the base.

widget.prompt: V(x) = 8000·bˣ halves each hour. Slide the base until b² reads 0.25.
widget.successFeedback: Base 0.5, so b² = 0.25 and V(2) = 8000 × 0.25 = 2000. A base below 1 is decay, and two halvings leave a quarter — not half of a half taken away, but half OF a half.
widget.lowFeedback: b² is below 0.25, so this decays faster than halving. Raise the base toward 0.5.
widget.highFeedback: b² is above 0.25 — slower than halving. Lower the base toward 0.5.

widget.prompt: A quantity grows 50% each year. Slide the base until b¹ shows the growth factor.
widget.successFeedback: 1.5 — the original whole plus half of it, in one multiplier. That is why a 50% rise is ×1.5 and not ×0.5: the base carries the original amount as well as the growth.
widget.lowFeedback: Below 1.5 this grows by less than 50% a year.
widget.highFeedback: Above 1.5 this grows by more than 50% a year.

widget.prompt: Solve 2ˣ = 8 by matching bases. Slide the base until b³ lands on 8.
widget.successFeedback: Base 2, because 2³ = 8. Matching bases works precisely because bˣ is one-to-one: once both sides read the same base, the exponents have no choice but to agree.
widget.lowFeedback: b³ is under 8 — raise the base.
widget.highFeedback: b³ is over 8 — lower the base.

widget.prompt: f(x) = 2·bˣ. Slide the base until b⁴ reads 16, then compare the curve with a straight line.
widget.successFeedback: Base 2 gives b⁴ = 16 and f(4) = 32. Watch the shape while you slide: a linear rule adds the same amount each step, this multiplies by the same amount — which is why it starts slower and finishes far ahead.

widget.prompt: Compounding more and more often drives the growth factor toward one particular number. Slide the base until b¹ lands near 2.7.
widget.successFeedback: ≈ 2.718 — the number e. It is not chosen for convenience: it is the limit that (1 + 1/n)ⁿ approaches as the compounding gets finer, and the only base whose curve rises exactly as fast as its own height.
widget.lowFeedback: Still below e — quarterly compounding gives 2.44, and finer compounding pushes higher.
widget.highFeedback: Past e now. The limit is about 2.718, and no compounding frequency exceeds it.

widget.prompt: ln(e⁷) asks which base makes log_b(e⁷) come out to exactly 7. Slide the base to find it.
widget.successFeedback: Base e ≈ 2.718, giving ln(e⁷) = 7. A logarithm asks 'what exponent?', so ln undoes eˣ exactly — the mirror line shows the two curves reflecting into each other.
widget.lowFeedback: With a base this small the logarithm reads too high.
widget.highFeedback: With a base this large the logarithm reads too low.

widget.prompt: x = log₇20 must lie between two whole numbers. Slide the base to 7 and read where log_b(20) lands.
widget.successFeedback: log₇20 ≈ 1.54, between 1 and 2 — because 7¹ = 7 is below 20 and 7² = 49 is above it. Bracketing a logarithm between the two nearest powers is the check that catches a wrong answer before any arithmetic.

widget.prompt: Build y = x² − 6x + 9 in vertex form, then look at where the vertex sits relative to the x-axis.
widget.successFeedback: y = (x − 3)², vertex (3, 0) — the vertex sits ON the axis, so the curve touches once and never crosses. That is a discriminant of exactly 0: 36 − 36 = 0. The sign of D is the position of the vertex.
widget.shapeFeedback: The a-value controls the opening; for x² − 5x + 6 it is 1, opening upward.
widget.vertexFeedback: Not there yet. x² − 6x + 9 is a perfect square, so the vertex sits on the axis at x = 3.

widget.prompt: x² − 4x − 12 = 0 becomes (x − 2)² = k. Build y = x² − 4x − 12 and read k off the vertex.
widget.successFeedback: Vertex (2, −16), so x² − 4x − 12 = (x − 2)² − 16 and (x − 2)² = 16. Half of −4 is −2, and squaring it is what moves the vertex — completing the square is locating the vertex, nothing more.
widget.shapeFeedback: Leave a at 1; the equation has no coefficient in front of x².
widget.vertexFeedback: Not there yet. Half of −4 is −2, so the vertex sits at x = 2.

widget.prompt: Build x² + 5x + 6 as a rectangle: drag the two partitions until the corner area reads 6, then read the middle coefficient.
widget.successFeedback: 2 and 3: the corner is 2 × 3 = 6 and the two strips total 2x + 3x = 5x. That is why factoring hunts for numbers that MULTIPLY to the constant and ADD to the middle — the rectangle makes both conditions visible at once.
widget.productMiddleFeedback: The corner area is right but the strips do not total 5x, or the reverse. Both conditions must hold together.
widget.partialFeedback: Keep dragging — the rectangle is not yet x² + 5x + 6.
widget.signFeedback: Both partitions are positive here, since the constant and the middle term are both positive.

widget.prompt: Build (x + 3)(x − 3) as a rectangle and watch what happens to the middle strips.
widget.successFeedback: +3 and −3: the strips are +3x and −3x, and they cancel. That cancellation is the whole difference-of-squares pattern — x² − 9 has no middle term because the two partitions are opposites.
widget.productMiddleFeedback: The corner is right but the strips are not cancelling. For a difference of squares the two partitions must be opposites.
widget.signFeedback: One partition must be positive and the other negative — that is what makes the middle vanish.

widget.prompt: P = 2L + 2W with P = 12 and L = 1 becomes 2W + 2 = 12. Clear the units, then split into equal groups.
widget.successFeedback: W = 5. Rearranging a formula is the same moves as solving a number equation — clear what is added, then undo the multiplication — which is why 'solve for W' needs no new rules, only the ones already in hand.
widget.unbalancedFeedback: The pans disagree. Whatever you remove from one side must come off the other.
widget.notIsolatedFeedback: W is not alone yet — there are still units on its pan.
widget.missFeedback: Not the solution. Clear the 2 units first, then split what remains into 2 equal groups.
widget.unexpandedFeedback: Deal with the added units before splitting into groups.

widget.prompt: A = bh/2 with A = 12 and b = 6 becomes 3h = 24 once both sides are doubled. Split into equal groups.
widget.successFeedback: h = 8. Doubling first cleared the fraction, and what was left was an ordinary one-step equation. Fractions in a formula are an obstacle to remove, not a different kind of problem.
widget.unbalancedFeedback: The pans disagree — the same operation must hit both sides.
widget.missFeedback: Not the solution. 3h = 24 splits into 3 equal groups.
widget.unexpandedFeedback: Split the pan into equal groups.

widget.prompt: Substituting y = 3x into 2x + y = 10 gives 5x = 10. Split into equal groups.
widget.successFeedback: x = 2, and then y = 3x = 6. Substitution earns its name here: replacing y turned a two-variable system into this single balance, and the second variable falls out afterwards for free.
widget.unbalancedFeedback: The pans disagree — operate on both sides.
widget.missFeedback: Not the solution. 5x = 10 splits into 5 equal groups.
widget.unexpandedFeedback: Split the pan into equal groups.

widget.prompt: For x − y = 1 and 2x + y = 8, adding the equations gives 3x = 9. Split into equal groups.
widget.successFeedback: x = 3, then y = 2. Adding the two equations made y disappear because its coefficients were opposites — the same balance move as always, applied to a whole equation rather than a number.
widget.missFeedback: Not the solution. 3x = 9 splits into 3 equal groups.
widget.unexpandedFeedback: Split the pan into equal groups.

widget.prompt: A book x and pen y cost $18, and the book is $4 more. Substituting y = x − 4 gives 2x − 4 = 18. Clear the units, then split.
widget.successFeedback: x = 11 and y = 7 — $11 book, $7 pen, together $18 with the book $4 dearer. Both checks matter: a solution to one equation that fails the other is not a solution to the system.
widget.notIsolatedFeedback: x is not alone yet — units remain on its pan.
widget.missFeedback: Not the solution. Add the 4 units back to both pans first, then split into 2 groups.
widget.unexpandedFeedback: Deal with the units before splitting into groups.

widget.prompt: 3 tickets cost $21, adults $8 and students $5. Substituting y = 3 − x gives 3x + 15 = 21. Clear the units, then split.
widget.successFeedback: x = 2 adult tickets, so 1 student ticket: 2×8 + 1×5 = 21 across 3 tickets. The 15 is what all three would cost at the student price; the 3 is the extra each adult ticket adds on top.
widget.missFeedback: Not the solution. Take the 15 units off both pans, then split what remains into 3 groups.

widget.prompt: Sweep the vertical line across the circle. Record the greatest number of crossings, then decide whether it is a function.
widget.successFeedback: Two crossings over most of the sweep, so it is not a function: an input with two outputs breaks the rule. The test is not a convention — it is the definition, drawn.
widget.moreSweepFeedback: Keep sweeping. One position proves nothing; the verdict depends on the worst case anywhere along the domain.
widget.verdictFeedback: Look again at the maximum crossing count you recorded. Two outputs for one input means not a function.

widget.prompt: 3, 7, 11, 15 grows by a fixed step. Dial the common difference until the 10th term lands on 39.
widget.successFeedback: d = 4: ten terms means nine gaps, so 3 + 9×4 = 39. Arithmetic sequences ADD a fixed amount — that is what separates them from geometric, which multiplies.
widget.lowFeedback: Too small — the 10th term falls short of 39.

refusals.title: Simplifying, combining and distributing radicals
refusals.why: Searched the manip>=2 catalogue for a surd engine. There is none: exactNumberLab (manip 1) is the corpus's radical surface, placeValueTransformLab's exponentChain handles integer exponent arithmetic rather than surd extraction, and no engine represents √72 = 6√2 as a manipulable state. These four are a genuine engine gap, not a fit failure — a `radicalSimplifyLab` would convert all four plus rad-03-03 and re-01-03. Refused pending that decision.

refusals.title: LCD, unlike denominators, horizontal asymptotes
refusals.why: The LCD lessons manipulate symbolic denominators, which no engine models — algebraTiles is integer-coefficient, binomialAreaLab is a product rectangle. For rf-04-03, graphZoom's behaviour enum is continuous|removable|jump|infinite, which is about discontinuity type rather than end-behaviour ratios. Refused.

refusals.title: Expand & condense, solving with e and ln, logarithmic scales
refusals.why: expLogExplore slides a BASE and reads one value; it cannot represent the product/quotient/power laws being applied symbolically (lg-02-03), a two-step solve (lg-04-03), or a ratio of two magnitudes on a log scale (lg-05-03). The engine fits 'which base' questions, and these are not those. Refused.

refusals.title: The Full Discriminant Story, Choosing the Best Method
refusals.why: Both are classification-over-methods lessons — sort each equation by root type, or by the method that solves it fastest. The thing being manipulated would have to be the choice itself. Same shape as the statistical-inference checklist refusals. Refused.
